Before I dive into full research, I want to flag one important structural issue and then get moving on the parts of this that are genuinely jurisdiction-neutral.

**Why this matters:** the Protean research-governance framework this system runs on is explicitly jurisdiction-scoped — regulatory status, licensing, and scope-of-practice claims must be tied to a specific country/subnational unit (`{{jurisdiction}}`). For "GP" specifically, this isn't a cosmetic detail: whether an AI system can legally "pre-assess" or "backfill" a doctor's diagnostic function is governed by completely different regimes depending on jurisdiction — e.g. FDA Software-as-a-Medical-Device rules (US), MHRA/UKCA medical device classification (UK), TGA regulation of clinical decision software (Australia), or the EU AI Act's high-risk classification for medical AI (EU). The clinical guideline bodies you'd ground diagnosis logic in also differ (NICE CKS/NICE guidelines in UK vs USPSTF/CDC in US vs RACGP in Australia vs WHO globally), and GP scope-of-practice/liability law differs by jurisdiction too.

So I'll do two things this turn: (1) run trusted-source web research now on the parts of this that are genuinely jurisdiction-agnostic — the underlying clinical-AI literature, ontologies, decision-support standards, and lineage/explainability requirements that apply regardless of country — and (2) ask you the one blocking question needed before I can responsibly ground the regulatory/licensing/clinical-guideline layer.

Before I do, here's my reasoning on how I've organized it and what's still missing.

**What I found and how I graded it:** I sorted everything into the same trust-tier model Protean uses for professional documentation (Tier 1 Primary Authority = regulators/statutory guidance; Tier 2 Institutional Authority = standards bodies, peer-reviewed literature, national health agencies; Tier 3 Context Support = preprints, vendor blogs, commentary — usable only for context, never as sole support). Two things fell out of that sorting that matter for how you build this:

1. The most relevant "how do we do this safely" source — the FDA's **Clinical Decision Support Software guidance** — was *itself updated on 2026-01-06*, which is after your reference date window and confirms this is a live-moving regulatory area, not settled ground.
2. The one paper that most directly matches your "full lineage" requirement (Alu & Oluwadare, *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence*, 2026-02-04) is explicitly a **conceptual/unvalidated framework** — the authors themselves say it has no empirical validation yet. I'm flagging that prominently rather than presenting it as proven, because presenting an untested architecture as settled practice would be exactly the kind of unsupported claim this system is built to prevent.

I also want to flag one preprint honestly: the "conversational diagnostic AI in ambulatory primary care" study (arXiv 2603.08448) is the closest real-world precedent to what you're describing, but it's an arXiv preprint — not peer-reviewed — so it belongs in Tier 3 only, and I could not extract its quantitative results from the fetch (the tool reported the PDF's numeric findings weren't cleanly extractable as text). That's a genuine limitation, not something I'm papering over.

<protean:artefact type="markdown" title="Trusted-Source Literature Base — AI Pre-Assessment Agent for GP Diagnostic Backfill">
# Trusted-Source Literature Base
## Grounding an AI Pre-Assessment Agent for General Practice (GP) Diagnostic Support

**Record type:** literature_grounding_survey (jurisdiction-neutral phase)
**Reference date:** 2026-08-03
**Research mode:** trusted_sources_only
**Governance status:** `partially_verified` — jurisdiction-specific regulatory, licensing, and clinical-guideline layers are **not yet resolved** (see Open Questions). Do not treat this as a complete, deployable record.

---

## 1. Purpose framing

This survey supports building an agent that: (a) conducts structured patient pre-assessment, (b) generates a ranked differential-diagnosis and next-steps briefing for a supervising GP, and (c) records complete decision lineage (source, retrieval, reasoning chain) for every claim. It deliberately stops short of proposing the agent *replace* diagnostic authority — every trusted source found treats human clinical sign-off as a hard requirement, not an optional feature.

---

## 2. Foundational literature by category

### 2.1 Ethics & governance (Tier 1/2 — primary and institutional authority)

| Source | Publisher | Date | Trust tier | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health* | WHO | 2021-06-28 | Tier 1 | Six global ethical principles for health AI; explicitly requires humans remain in control of medical decisions. First global framework of its kind — foundational for any "backfill" design. |
| WHO 2024 guidance on large multi-modal models (LMMs) in health | WHO | 2024 | Tier 1 | 40+ recommendations specific to generative/LLM-based tools; addresses hallucination risk directly — core relevance to "grounded in truth" requirement. |

### 2.2 Regulatory classification of the software itself (Tier 1)

| Source | Publisher | Date | Trust tier | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global Approach to SaMD | FDA / IMDRF | ongoing (2013 framework origin) | Tier 1 | International definitional framework for Software as a Medical Device — determines whether your agent is regulated as a medical device at all. |
| Clinical Decision Support Software – Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff | FDA | updated 2026-01-06 | Tier 1 | US-specific: draws the exact line between exempt CDS (displays info, doesn't replace judgment, transparent logic) and regulated SaMD. Directly determines legal posture of a "pre-assessment + rundown" tool in the US. |
| Good Machine Learning Practice for Medical Device Development: Guiding Principles | FDA + Health Canada + UK MHRA | 2021-10 | Tier 1 (tri-national) | 10 principles for ML-enabled medical devices — data quality, algorithm robustness, update handling. Jointly issued by three national regulators, so has cross-jurisdiction weight even though each still applies its own law. |
| Transparency for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices: Guiding Principles | FDA | 2024-06 | Tier 1 | Explainability/disclosure requirements: training-data characteristics, subgroup performance, update history must be communicated to users — directly maps to your "lineage" requirement. |

### 2.3 Terminology / ontology grounding (Tier 1)

| Source | Publisher | Trust tier | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| SNOMED CT | SNOMED International (IHTSDO) | Tier 1 | ~330,000 clinical concepts; the terminology layer any grounded diagnostic reasoning engine should anchor to, so claims are traceable to a controlled vocabulary rather than free text. |
| ICD-11 | WHO | Tier 1 | Statistical/classificatory backbone; WHO coordinates cross-mapping with SNOMED and LOINC for interoperability. |
| LOINC | Regenstrief Institute + SNOMED International | Tier 1 | Standardises the *questions* (observations/tests) where SNOMED CT standardises the *answers* (findings/diagnoses) — both needed for a coherent pre-assessment data model. |

### 2.4 Evidence-base / knowledge sources for grounding claims (Tier 2)

| Source | Publisher | Trust tier | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cochrane Systematic Reviews / Cochrane Clinical Answers | Cochrane Collaboration | Tier 1 (systematic review primary evidence) | Highest tier of the evidence pyramid; feeds into BMJ Best Practice. |
| BMJ Best Practice | BMJ | Tier 2 | Point-of-care tool structured around the *consultation* (symptom evaluation → tests → treatment), explicit EBM grading, links to Cochrane. Structurally close to what a pre-assessment agent needs to reproduce. |
| DynaMed | EBSCO | Tier 2 | Uses explicit GRADE levels of evidence per recommendation — good candidate for a machine-readable evidence-grading layer. |
| UpToDate | Wolters Kluwer | Tier 2 | GRADE-style ratings; widely used point-of-care reference in US clinical settings. |
| "6S Pyramid" evidence hierarchy model | McMaster University Health Sciences Library | Tier 2 | Formal EBM hierarchy (Studies → Syntheses → Synopses → Summaries → Systems) — useful as the architectural model for how the agent should rank/cite evidence quality per claim. |

### 2.5 Pre-assessment / triage protocols (Tier 2, protocol-specific — note below)

| Source | Trust tier | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Manchester Triage System | Tier 2 (proprietary clinical protocol, peer-reviewed validation literature) | Five-level, flowchart/discriminator-based urgency model (immediate → non-urgent), colour-coded max wait times. A structured, auditable decision-tree model — good template for explainable triage logic. |
| Emergency Severity Index (ESI), current handbook edition | Tier 2 (US emergency medicine, AHRQ-linked) | Alternative five-level acuity+resource-need model, most common alternative to MTS. |
| **Limitation noted:** search results returned peer-reviewed *comparative validation studies* of MTS/ESI rather than the primary protocol documents themselves — the original developer/owner documents should be sourced directly before implementation. |  |  |

### 2.6 AI clinical-reasoning literature (Tier 2/3 — mixed, see caveats)

| Source | Type | Trust tier | Key point / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Impact of AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems on Diagnostic Accuracy" — systematic review & meta-analysis of RCTs, *MDPI Applied Sciences* | Peer-reviewed systematic review | Tier 2 | Best current evidence tier on whether AI-CDS actually improves diagnostic accuracy — cite this over any vendor claim. |
| "Effects of a Differential Diagnosis List of AI on Differential Diagnoses by Physicians" — RCT sub-analysis, PMC | Peer-reviewed RCT analysis | Tier 2 | Direct empirical evidence on how AI-generated differential lists change physician diagnostic behaviour — relevant to your "rundown to the doctor" design. |
| "Evidence-based XAI of clinical decision support systems for differential diagnosis" | medRxiv **preprint** | Tier 3 (not peer-reviewed) | Explainable-AI design pattern: links each predicted disease back to sourced case data/literature — architecturally relevant to lineage design, but **not peer-reviewed**, use for design inspiration only, not as authority. |
| "An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating RAG with data provenance" — *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence*, Alu & Oluwadare, 2026-02-04 | Peer-reviewed, but **conceptual/proposal paper** | Tier 2 (journal) with an explicit caveat | Closest match to your "full lineage" requirement. Architecture: curated sources with GRADE-level provenance metadata → RAG retrieval with confidence scoring and post-hoc claim verification → **immutable, tamper-evident audit log** (permissioned ledger) recording query, retrieved documents, inference chain, cryptographic hash of patient data, timestamp, user ID. **Authors state this is untested — no empirical validation exists yet.** Do not present as proven practice. |
| "A prospective clinical feasibility study of a conversational diagnostic AI in an ambulatory primary care clinic" | arXiv **preprint** | Tier 3 (not peer-reviewed) | Direct real-world precedent: conversational AI gathers history pre-visit, generates differential diagnosis, hands off to physician under human-in-the-loop oversight. **Could not extract quantitative results from the fetched PDF this turn** — flagging as an open item rather than fabricating outcome figures. |

### 2.7 Liability / oversight literature (Tier 1/2)

| Source | Trust tier | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| WHO 2021 guidance (autonomy principle) | Tier 1 | Final decision authority must remain human. |
| EU AI Act — high-risk classification of diagnostic AI | Tier 1 (legislation) | Diagnostic AI is high-risk category; mandates ongoing human oversight as a condition of lawful deployment (EU-specific — not yet confirmed applicable to your target jurisdiction). |
| *Nature* commentary, "When physicians and AI work together, who is accountable?" | Tier 3 (editorial/commentary) | Frames the accountability question but is not itself a legal authority — use only as context, not as the governing source. |
| US state-law commentary on AI diagnosis liability (law-firm sources) | Tier 3 | Explicitly excluded from serving as sole authority per this system's sourcing policy — flagged here only to show the topic exists; actual liability rules must come from the relevant state's statutes/case law directly. |

---

## 3. What this survey establishes clearly (cross-source consensus)

1. Every authoritative source (WHO, FDA, EU AI Act) converges on **human-in-the-loop as a non-negotiable design constraint** — "backfill" cannot mean autonomous diagnostic authority without triggering high-risk/regulated-medical-device status almost everywhere.
2. Whether your agent is a *regulated medical device* at all turns on a narrow, jurisdiction-specific test (e.g., the FDA's exact CDS exemption criteria: no image/signal processing, transparent logic, supports rather than replaces judgment).
3. A credible "lineage" architecture (provenance-tagged sources, GRADE-style evidence grading, immutable audit logging, confidence scoring, post-hoc claim verification) exists in the literature **as a conceptual proposal**, not as a validated, deployed reference implementation.
4. Structured, explainable triage frameworks (MTS, ESI) already provide auditable decision-tree templates that predate AI and could underpin the pre-assessment layer's rule-based core, with AI reserved for the differential-diagnosis narrative layer.

## 4. Explicit limitations (per governance rules — not hidden in the record)

- No jurisdiction was specified, so **no licensing, GP scope-of-practice, or medical-device-classification claim in this survey should be treated as settled for any specific country**. FDA/US material dominates because it is the most publicly documented; do not assume it transfers to UK, EU, Australia, or elsewhere.
- Two Tier 3 preprints were included for architectural insight only (medRxiv XAI paper; arXiv primary-care conversational-AI study) and must not be cited as proof of safety or efficacy.
- The lead lineage-architecture paper (Alu & Oluwadare, 2026) is unvalidated by its own authors' admission.
- Primary MTS/ESI protocol documents were not directly retrieved — only peer-reviewed validation studies referencing them.

---

Now, the reason I have to stop before treating this as knowledge-base-ready: this system's governance rules require jurisdiction-specific grounding for anything touching regulation, licensing, or scope of practice — and for a GP-backfill agent, that's not a peripheral detail, it's the difference between "compliant clinical decision support tool" and "unregistered medical device practicing medicine without a license." **Confirmed live this turn (5 of the 23 sources in last turn's list):**
- FDA GMLP PDF (`fda.gov/media/153486/download`) → **direct PDF, no block.** Confirmed 440.4KB, valid document, metadata shows original author/date.

I traced it: `nature.com` → `idp.nature.com/authorize` → `idp.nature.com/transit` → back to `nature.com` with `?error=cookies_not_supported`. That's an SSO cookie-bounce loop that fails for any stateless fetcher (no browser, no cookie jar) — it may well be free to a human in a real browser, but no script (mine or otherwise) can complete it without emulating a persistent-cookie session. I'm not going to build cookie/session spoofing to force it through — that crosses from "polite retrieval" into "evading an access control," which I won't do even for a Tier 3 context-only source. **Not tested live this turn** (WHO `iris.who.int`, WHO `who.int/publications`, FDA HTML pages, ICD-11 FAQ, SNOMED docs, PMC terminology/triage/differential-diagnosis articles, McMaster 6S pyramid, medRxiv preprint, ESI handbook PDF at `sgnor.ch`) — I'm including these in the manifest because they came from last turn's grounded search, but I have **not** verified this turn whether each is bot-blockable. That's exactly why the script below doesn't just download-and-trust: it logs an HTTP status, a redirect/auth-wall detection flag, and a checksum for every single item, so the lineage record tells you definitively — the moment you run it — which of the untested 18 succeed and which need manual retrieval. I'm not asserting they all work; the script is designed to find out and record the truth rather than have me guess.

Design decisions worth flagging explicitly:

1. **robots.txt is checked and respected per-domain before downloading.** If a domain disallows the path, the script logs `robots_disallowed` and skips rather than overriding it. Circumventing robots.txt for a literature-grounding tool would undermine the "trusted source" premise of the whole system.
2. **No browser/cookie emulation, no fake-browser User-Agent spoofing.** The script identifies itself honestly (`Protean-LiteratureIngest/1.0`). If a server blocks an honest research client, that's a real signal to record and route to manual review — not something to engineer around.
3. **Full lineage per item**: SHA-256 checksum, HTTP status, final URL after redirects, content-type, byte count, ISO timestamp, trust tier, and a status enum (`downloaded`, `manual_review_required`, `http_error`, `robots_disallowed`). Written to both JSON (machine-ingestible) and CSV (human-reviewable).
4. **Idempotent**: re-running skips files already downloaded with a matching hash, unless `--force` is passed.
5. **Rate-limited** (default 3s between requests) — polite to the government/journal servers you're pulling from, and reduces the chance of triggering rate-based blocking in the first place.That's a genuinely useful data point — **medRxiv returned a real HTTP 403 to this tool just now**, which is precisely the "bot being blocked" scenario you described, and it's a different failure mode from Nature's cookie-loop: this is a direct server-side block, not a session problem. You're right, and I should have led with this distinction last turn instead of building a governance-literature survey. Let me be precise about the error I made and then actually fix it.

**The error:** I built a literature base about *AI systems that touch healthcare* (SaMD regulation, XAI architecture papers, AI ethics guidance, RCT studies of AI-CDS tools). That is meta-commentary — it tells you how regulators think about AI, not what a doctor actually knows. An agent that is supposed to pre-assess a patient and hand a GP a differential diagnosis needs to be grounded in the same substrate a real doctor's brain is grounded in: pathophysiology, semiology (sign/symptom → disease mapping), diagnostic criteria, treatment algorithms, and the exact curricula/exam content that medical boards use to certify that a human knows this material. None of last turn's sources teach an agent to actually reason about a fever + rash + joint pain. That's the gap, and it's the right thing to be angry about — governance papers don't diagnose anyone.

I'm going to search now for the actual hard-clinical-knowledge sources: the open, authoritative repositories of clinical medical content, plus the certification/curriculum documents that define what a doctor is examined on, so the agent's knowledge base is built on the same ground truth as the human it's meant to backfill.Good — those searches confirm real, hard clinical/educational substrate exists and is trusted-source-gradeable. Before I compile it, let me check the actual bulk-access/licensing terms for the two biggest content repositories (StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf and NICE CKS), since last turn was about building a download pipeline — there's no point recommending a source I then can't legally or technically bulk-ingest.That licensing check turned up the single most important finding of this entire conversation, and it's not good news for the "just scrape it" approach — so I'm going to lead with it rather than bury it in a footnote.

**The hard truth about hard clinical truth:** almost every serious repository of actual clinical knowledge — the stuff a doctor is examined on, not commentary about AI — carries an explicit legal restriction on exactly the kind of automated ingestion a knowledge-base agent needs:

- **Merck Manual Professional** — free to *read*, but its Terms of Use explicitly prohibit "scrape, data mine, extract, view, access or download any data, content or materials" for purposes **"including training artificial intelligence models and large language models."** That's not ambiguous. I will not write a scraper against that source. Full stop.
- **StatPearls (hosted on NCBI Bookshelf, NIH/NLM)** — genuinely free, peer-reviewed, PubMed-indexed — but licensed **CC BY-NC-ND 4.0**. NC = no commercial use. ND = **no derivative works** — and chunking/embedding/re-summarizing content into a RAG knowledge base is arguably exactly what "no derivatives" is meant to stop. This forecloses it for any agent that will ever be deployed commercially, and puts even non-commercial use in a real legal grey zone the moment you transform the text.
- **NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS)** — copyright of Clarity Informatics/Agilio Software, gated behind an End User Licence Agreement. Free only for NHS staff and students for personal study; **explicitly requires a paid commercial/institutional licence for "any company, business, or other private enterprise, including universities."** An agent product is squarely in that category.

So: the reason last turn's problem looked like "bots are being blocked" is, for the highest-value sources, actually **"the rights holder has deliberately and explicitly forbidden this use."** No amount of politer scripting, better User-Agents, or retry logic fixes that — this is a rights question, not a networking question, and Protean's own rule against workarounds means I won't design around it. That's the correction I owe you on top of the subject-matter correction.

**The uncomfortable conclusion:** there is no free, legal, bulk-scrapeable single source that is simultaneously (a) authoritative hard clinical content, (b) structured like a GP consultation, and (c) unrestricted for commercial AI ingestion. The two sources structured most usefully for a GP pre-assessment agent (Merck Manual, NICE CKS) are the two with the hardest legal walls. This is a genuine constraint on the project, not a technical inconvenience to be engineered around.
